Using the Beige Book as a cross-check, the overall picture is an adverse supply-shock environment (pandemic aftereffects, higher energy prices, Ukraine war, and China lockdowns) keeping inflation elevated and posing downside risks to growth. District reports highlight widespread price pressures, persistent supply-chain backlogs, and acute worker shortages fueling strong wage growth. At the same time, the Beige Book indicates activity was still expanding in many Districts: consumer spending and manufacturing continued to contribute to growth, though autos were constrained by low inventories and some interest-sensitive segments were starting to cool. Credit conditions in early Q2 remained supportive per SLOOS: banks generally eased standards for C&I (especially large/middle-market firms) and multifamily CRE, saw stronger loan demand (inventories, receivables, equipment, plant), and eased consumer credit (e.g., cards), with firmer demand for HELOCs and autos but softer residential mortgage demand. Against this backdrop, the Fed tightened policy by 50 bp to 0.75–1% and began balance-sheet reduction, reflecting high inflation risks.

Net assessment: risks remain tilted to the downside due to inflation and supply disruptions, but ongoing spending/manufacturing momentum and supportive bank credit temper the negativity. Adjusting for Beige Book insights, the tone moves from negative to cautiously negative, slightly less downbeat than a read based on the FOMC statement alone.
